query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Graphene shell encapsulation governs the preservation of the structural and chemical integrity of near‐equiatomic HEA nanoparticles under high-temperature oxidative conditions by acting as a barrier that limits oxidation driven by the intrinsic redox potentials of the constituent elements.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution HEA nanoparticles, some of which are synthesized with a conformal graphene shell encapsulation.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of HEA nanoparticles: one with the graphene shell intact (using laser solid-phase synthesis on LIG supports) and a second where the graphene encapsulation is removed or not applied.
generation.conditions: Expose both sets to high-temperature operational ranges (773–1173 K for catalytic, and up to 1923 K for thermoelectric applications) in a controlled oxidative atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: The presence (or absence) of a graphene shell acting as a physical barrier against oxidation.
generation.mechanism: In the intact nanoparticles, the graphene shell inhibits oxygen access, thereby preventing preferential oxidation of elements with high redox potential (as influenced by atomic size and redox properties), which would otherwise cause compositional inversion and structural degradation. Without the graphene shell, the oxidation mechanism governed by these intrinsic properties proceeds unchecked.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with the graphene shell will retain their near-equiatomic composition and structural integrity, whereas those without the shell will exhibit rapid surface oxidation, compositional inversion, and associated degradation of catalytic/thermoelectric performance.
generation.baseline: Graphene shell encapsulated HEA nanoparticles exposed to the same high-temperature oxidative conditions.
generation.boundary: The protective effect of graphene encapsulation is expected to be significant within the tested temperature and oxidative regimes; outside these regimes (e.g., at significantly lower temperatures or in inert atmospheres), the difference between encapsulated and non-encapsulated particles may be negligible.
generation.uncertainty: The relative contributions of atomic size versus redox potential in driving the oxidation process in unencapsulated particles remain uncertain, and potential substrate effects or other synthesis-related variables might also influence the oxidation behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two identical batches of equiatomic HEA nanoparticles, with the only difference being the presence (unaltered) or deliberate removal of the graphene encapsulation. Subject both batches to prolonged exposure (e.g., several hours) at temperatures ranging from 773 to 1173 K in a controlled oxygen atmosphere.
measurements: Surface composition analysis via atom probe tomography to detect compositional inversion or preferential oxidation.
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) to evaluate structural changes and oxide layer formation.
Performance tests relevant to catalytic or thermoelectric functions to correlate structural integrity with functional performance.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the removal of the graphene encapsulation does not result in a statistically significant increase in oxidation, compositional inversion, or degradation of nanoparticle performance compared to encapsulated nanoparticles, then the hypothesis that graphene shells are the primary mediator of stability is falsified.

## Abstract
Complex multi-element alloys are gaining prominence for structural applications, supplementing steels, and superalloys. Understanding the impact of each element on alloy surfaces due to oxidation is vital in maintaining material integrity. This study investigates oxidation mechanisms in these alloys using a model five-element equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy, in a controlled oxygen environment. The oxidation-induced surface changes correlate with each element’s interactive tendencies with the environment, guided by thermodynamics. Initial oxidation stages follow atomic size and redox potential, with the latter becoming dominant over time, causing composition inversion. The study employs in-situ atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure techniques to elucidate the oxidation process and surface oxide structure evolution. Our findings deconvolute the mechanism for compositional and structural changes in the oxide film and will pave the way for a predictive design of complex alloys with improved resistance to oxidation under extreme conditions. ## Abstract
AbstractRapid synthesis of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA NPs) offers new opportunities to develop functional materials in widespread applications. Although some methods have successfully produced HEA NPs, these methods generally require rigorous conditions such as high pressure, high temperature, restricted atmosphere, and limited substrates, which impede practical viability. In this work, we report laser solid-phase synthesis of CrMnFeCoNi nanoparticles by laser irradiation of mixed metal precursors on a laser-induced graphene (LIG) support with a 3D porous structure. The CrMnFeCoNi nanoparticles are embraced by several graphene layers, forming graphene shell-encapsulated HEA nanoparticles. The mechanisms of the laser solid-phase synthesis of HEA NPs on LIG supports are investigated through theoretical simulation and experimental observations, in consideration of mixed metal precursor adsorption, thermal decomposition, reduction through electrons from laser-induced thermionic emission, and liquid beads splitting.
